title: LLMs and Valuation - Findings and Methodology
author: Kind_Soup_5285
selftext:
I was curious whether LLMs can be used for automatic valuation of stocks, and how helpful would that be to my investment process. [Here](https://undecidedmantis.substack.com/p/can-llms-actually-value-stocks) is a write-up of my research. Feedback welcome!

# Conclusion

(1) The LLM's ability to make connections between seemingly disparate ideas can make them uncover insights not widely appreciated by humans;

(2) The AI system needs to be designed for legibility (defined in article above) in order for humans to understand what's going on; and

(3) Humans need to ask the right questions as the LLMs currently favours spending time on easy questions rather than important ones.

# Notes

Note 1: I iterated for a few months and the final version presented in the report above is probably close to the ceiling of performance without training your own specialized LLM.

Note 2: Every investor's process is somewhat different, this system reflects my own. However, I think this is still useful to other fundamental investors as the type of questions we ask tend to be similar when looking at stocks.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: one thing to check before trusting it: the model may already know how each past story ended, since the later prices and headlines sit in its training data. did you score it only on calls made after its training cutoff?

replies.author: Kind_Soup_5285
replies.body: Valuation is done on live information in the present, so no one knows how the story ends, and definitely not in training data

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: for a live call, sure. in a backtest though the model is valuing 2019 with 2024 already in its weights, so it does know the ending. I built a backtester, Quantradin, mostly to stop that kind of leak in written rules (fake money, free, quantradin.com).

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I read the write-up. Keeping the model blind to the stock price and testing on a microcap like NamSys that it can't have memorized are good choices. Three companies scored by one person on a rubric is a small test, though, so one way to get an outside check is to freeze these valuations and compare them with the actual earnings in a year or two. The finding that it spends effort on easy questions and misses the important ones (like competitors and AI risk) also reads as the main limit, so logging which questions it chose would show it directly. Cymetica's Event Cards come with a sourced report for each news event, which is a similar idea of keeping the reasoning checkable.

comments.author: Express-Idea-8390
comments.body: The point about LLMs spending too much effort on easy questions is spot on. A model can generate an impressive valuation report while barely examining the one assumption that determines whether the stock is actually cheap. I'd want every conclusion linked to its input data. Moon is where I take simpler speculative price views but for fundamental research the ability to challenge the reasoning is much more important than polished writing.
